newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul's refugee welcome mat is getting frayed.
newsitem.headline: Seoul's refugee welcome mat is getting frayed.

text.p: When a North Korean MiG-19 pilot defected in May, Seoul laid out the red carpet. The reception for a half-starved brick factory worker fished out of the sea was less rapturous.
Now a whole Northern family has pitched up, and while Seoul is not turning anyone away, the welcoming arms are not spreading quite as readily for everyone.
Suddenly, South Koreans are facing up to a potential refugee nightmare: an uncontrolled tide of hungry, desperate North Koreans flooding across the border and swamping the country's resources.
Beyond the practical problems -- feeding, housing, employing ragged "freedom seekers" -- lies the even more terrifying prospect of armed conflict.

In various crisis scenarios mapped out by South Korea, a refugee stampede is a potential trigger for a war. Would Northern border guards shoot-to-kill fleeing countrymen? If so, would Southern troops stand back and watch, or jump in and risk a military blow-up.
The 17 North Koreans who arrived from Hong Kong on Monday after a month-long trek through China included 16 members of a single family and a security guard.
They were the biggest group of escapees since the 1950-53 Korean War, which sealed the World War Two split of the Korean peninsula, and brought to 51 the number of defectors to South Korea this year.
Last year, 38 made it across the border and in 1994 a total of 50 landed.
While the numbers are not great, the escape of 17 together has had the shock effect in Seoul of a mass breakout from a maximum-security jail.

Previous solo flights -- or escapes in twos and threes -- were put down to bravery and cunning. An entire clan, reportedly including a pregnant woman, has suggested to some a breakdown of internal controls in North Korea, which has been devastated by floods and industrial collapse.

A party that large, it is thought, could not simply trick their way into China: border guards must have been bought off, police paid to look the other way, officials bribed for transport tickets and travel passes.
"It shows a phenomenal level of organisation," said one Seoul-based Western diplomat.
So far there is no indication of the kind of mass internal migrations in North Korea that could signal the collapse of the world's last Stalinist outpost.
And, said the diplomat, the recent defectors come from such widely different backgrounds -- including a drama script writer and a pharmacist -- it is hard to draw conclusions.
"You're still only talking about hundreds, not millions," he said. North Korea has a population of 23 million.
Yet Southern authorities are preparing for a much larger-scale exodus than anything so far.

The Ministry of National Unification is drawing up blueprints for reception centres -- half-way houses offering food and shelter and vocational training -- with the first possibly opening its doors next year.

Ironically, having spent the Cold War fretting about Pyongyang's military might, South Korea and its ally the United States now think the biggest threat is North Korea's weakness, which may tempt it to lash out in a final desperate gamble.
Refugee flows are a good measure of the North's decrepitude.

Signs of a higher outflow have set off alarm bells among North Korea's neighbours. China fears a refugee army marching across its borders; Japan has visions of a flotilla of refugee boats setting sail for its shores.

But no country has more reason to feel scared than South Korea, which would be left to pick up the pieces from any North Korean collapse and has been praying for a "soft landing" for its troubled neighbour.
The costs to Seoul of Korean unification, if North Korea crumbled like the former East Germany, start at $600 billion by some estimates and go as high as $3 trillion.
